text: The arbitrium system, discovered by Erez et al. (2017) in Bacillus phages, is significant because it demonstrates that:
choices: Bacteriophages communicate with one another using a secreted peptide that reports on prior population activity, and use it to modulate the lysis-lysogeny decision
Viruses contain miniature neurons that process information
Temperate phages can only ever replicate lytically, never lysogenically
The lysis-lysogeny decision is made entirely at random with no molecular basis
explanation: Arbitrium is effectively 'viral quorum sensing': infecting phages secrete a small peptide that accumulates with lytic activity and is read by later-infecting phages to bias their lysis-versus-lysogeny choice, transmitting population-level information across infections. Viruses have no neurons (option 1); temperate phages can do both lysis and lysogeny (option 2); and while the choice is stochastic, in lambda it is governed by the competing CI repressor and Cro proteins, not pure randomness (option 3).
